summary: The cluster is cheap: about 9 s per run (KnightsTest 3.6 s, KnightsDataTest 1.0 s, ClausifyTest 1.1 s, KnightsTestMinimal 1.0 s, PlutusScriptEvaluatorTest 0.9 s, the rest under 0.5 s); the benchmark suites pin budgets on purpose, so the only ci-time wins are duplicate tests (C15-12, C15-13). The bloxbean module is weakly tested: 19.3% statement and 10.1% branch coverage. Interop's ScriptContext path, ScalusTransactionEvaluator and the CCL suppliers have no unit test, and the three *BlocksLedgerTest suites silently skip 685 of 712 block txs because only 27 have UTxOs in /utxos. One main-code defect: Interop.toPlutusData loses Data.Map entry order for maps with more than 4 entries and drops duplicate keys (C15-5); InteropMapOrderingTest cannot see it because CCL encodes CBOR canonically and the test keys are pre-sorted. The benchmark files are dominated by dead Options branches and a 940-line hand-nested Cons literal (C15-16, C15-17). The sbt plugin tests (BlueprintLayout, LeanLayout) are adequate. No generators in the cluster (C8: only the Arbitrary[Data] proposed in C15-6, which never makes duplicate map keys).

findings.claim: The three *BlocksLedgerTest suites check almost nothing. The loop catches 'UTXO not found for input' and skips the tx (46-52). /utxos holds 100 files, so only 27 of the 712 txs in the 25 committed blocks resolve (counted by decoding the blocks with a scratch CBOR reader): blocks 11544518, 11544748 and 11553070 give 9+3+15; the other 22 blocks give 0. MetadataValidator and ScriptsWellFormedValidator do not read state.utxos at all (ScriptsWellFormedValidator binds it at line 14 and never uses it), yet they are skipped for the same 685 txs. A rule that rejects every tx outside those 3 blocks still passes; if /utxos is lost, all three suites pass while they check 0 txs.
findings.action: Give BlocksLedgerRulesValidator a constructor flag needsUtxos (false for MetadataValidator and ScriptsWellFormedValidator). When it is false, do not resolve UTxOs, so the rule runs on all 712 txs. When it is true, count the txs the rule checked and assert the count equals a pinned number (27 today). Remove the commented-out printlns at 34, 42-44, 50-52.
findings.coverageRisk: none: adds checks. 685 txs are new for two rules; a failure there is a real rule or decoding defect to triage, not a test bug.

findings.claim: The script is (one, two) => one + two, applied to 1 and 2. Addition is commutative, so a mutation that applies the params in reverse order (iterate params from the end, the main risk of applyParamsToScript) still gives 3.
findings.action: Compile (one, two) => one.toBigInt - two.toBigInt and expect -1 in both tests (or 10*one + two and expect 12).

findings.claim: By reading (not executed): Interop.toPlutusData(Data.Map(items)) builds the CCL map with items...toMap.asJava. A Scala immutable Map with more than 4 entries is a HashMap, so the MapPlutusData iterates in hash order, not in the Data.Map entry order; duplicate keys, which Plutus maps allow, are silently dropped. A Data.Map with keys I(5), I(4), I(3), I(2), I(1) gives a MapPlutusData whose getMap.keySet is not in that order; Data.Map([(I 1, I 0), (I 1, I 1)]) gives 1 entry. Any non-canonical datum, or a datum with a repeated key, converted to CCL gets a different hash. The InteropMapOrderingTest round trip cannot see it: CCL's serializeToBytes encodes canonically (CborSerializationUtil.serialize defaults to canonical = true, cardano-client-common 0.7.3), which re-sorts the keys, and both tests feed already sorted keys.
findings.action: Main-code note only: fill a java.util.LinkedHashMap in entry order instead of .toMap.asJava, and document (or reject) duplicate keys, which a java.util.Map cannot hold. Test: see C15-6.
findings.coverageRisk: none: a finding, not a test change
findings.verification:
The defect is real. Interop.scala:190-201 passes `items...toMap.asJava` into the Lombok `MapPlutusData.builder().map(...)`. That builder stores the given map as-is (MapPlutusData.java in cardano-client-plutus 0.7.3: `@Builder.Default map = new LinkedHashMap<>()`, which the builder overrides). A Scala Map with more than 4 entries is a HashMap, so `getMap` iterates in hash order. Duplicate keys are dropped by `.toMap`. Any user can reach this through the public `Interop.toPlutusData`; no main code calls it (grep finds only Interop.scala).

The hash consequence is overstated. CCL hashes and serializes canonically by default: `PlutusData.getDatumHashAsBytes` and `serializeToBytes` call `CborSerializationUtil.serialize(DataItem)`, which sets canonical=true (CborSerializationUtil.java:124-126). `CustomMapEncoder.java:45,79` then re-sorts keys in a TreeMap and also merges equal keys. `Transaction.serialize` is canonical too (Transaction.java:117). So the order loss does not change CCL's datum hash. A non-canonical datum gets a different CCL hash even after the fix. Duplicate keys are lost by any java.util.Map, and the canonical TreeMap would merge them anyway.

Corrected claim: toPlutusData loses Data.Map entry order in `MapPlutusData.getMap` for maps with more than 4 entries. Only code that iterates getMap, or that serializes with `serialize(x, false)`, can see this. Fix it with a LinkedHashMap filled in entry order. Document that duplicate keys cannot be kept, because a java.util.Map cannot hold them and CCL canonical CBOR merges them anyway.

findings.claim: The two tests are instances of one law: Data -> PlutusData -> Data is the identity. Test 1 (5 sorted 32-byte keys) is a subset of test 2 (10 sorted keys, 4 of them shared) and asserts the same thing. Both go through canonical CBOR, which hides toPlutusData's order loss (C15-5).
findings.action: Replace both tests with forAll { (d: Data) => Interop.toScalusData(Interop.toPlutusData(d)) == d } using arbData from scalus.uplc.test.ArbitraryInstances (in-memory, no CBOR). Add explicit examples for a 6-entry map with descending keys and a map with a duplicate key. Build change: add scalusTestkit.jvm % Test (or scalacheck) to scalus-bloxbean-cardano-client-lib. arbData uses Gen.mapOfN, so it never makes duplicate keys (hence the explicit example). The property fails until C15-5 is fixed; mark it pending or land it with the fix.
findings.coverageRisk: low: the CBOR round trip through CCL's deserializer goes away; keep one CBOR example if CCL decode order matters (it is what commit a8a713232 fixed in toScalusData).
findings.verification:
The law Data -> PlutusData -> Data == id mostly holds in memory once C15-5 is fixed:
- Constr tags are `Gen.posNum[Long]` (ArbitraryInstances.scala:107), so `ConstrPlutusData.alternative: long` holds them.
- Map keys come from `Gen.mapOfN`, so they are distinct (ArbitraryInstances.scala:120-124).
- arbData is reachable from this module through scalusTestkit, which copies ArbitraryInstances into its src_managed.

There is one rare counterexample even after the fix. `MapPlutusData` uses `@EqualsAndHashCode` over a java.util.Map, and that equality ignores order. So an outer map whose keys are two Data.Maps that differ only in entry order loses one entry. Generating this is very unlikely.

The claim has a minor error: test 1's 5 keys are all among test 2's 10 keys (5 shared, not 4). So test 1 really is a subset of test 2 (InteropMapOrderingTest.scala:13-22 vs 70-80).

The in-memory property skips the path that commit a8a713232 fixed. That path is `PlutusData.deserialize` (MapPlutusData.deserialize builds a LinkedHashMap) followed by `toScalusData`, which is how datums from the chain arrive. Keeping a CBOR example must be required, not optional.

Corrected action:
- Delete test 1 (lines 11-66).
- Keep test 2 (lines 68-109) as the CBOR decode-order regression test.
- Add the in-memory forAll property only together with the C15-5 LinkedHashMap fix.
- Add explicit examples for a map with more than 4 entries in descending order and for a duplicate key (expect it to collapse, as documented).

findings.claim: BlockDeserializationTest only checks that BlockFile.fromCborArray does not throw on 3 blocks. BlocksLedgerRulesValidator decodes every file in /blocks/ (all 25, including 11544748, 11544518 and 11649988) outside its try block, in each of its 3 suites, so a decode failure already fails them; PlutusScriptEvaluatorTest decodes 2 of the 3 again and asserts their tx counts. The ignored test (23-29) reads ./blocks, which does not exist in the repository.
findings.coverageRisk: low: decode coverage of all 25 blocks stays in the *BlocksLedgerTest suites; it would be lost if those suites are removed later
findings.verification:
BlockDeserializationTest.scala:11-21 has 3 tests. Each only calls `BlockFile.fromCborArray(bytes)` on block-11544748, 11544518 and 11649988, and none of them asserts anything. The ignored test (lines 23-29) reads `./blocks`, which is not in the repo.

The same entry point is used elsewhere, outside any try block. BlocksLedgerRulesValidator.scala:19-29 runs `Files.list(/blocks/)` over all 25 resources (all 3 blocks are present), and line 29 calls `BlockFile.fromCborArray(bytes)`. A decode failure therefore fails the suite. `fromCborArray` takes no `using` parameter and sets OriginalCborByteArray itself (Block.scala:98-100), so the caller's given makes no difference.

Three active suites extend this validator:
- MetadataValidatorBlocksLedgerTest
- ScriptsWellFormedValidatorBlocksLedgerTest
- ProtocolParamsViewHashesMatchValidatorBlocksLedgerTest

CardanoMutatorBlocksLedgerTest is commented out. All three suites are in the same module, so they run in the same CI jobs.

PlutusScriptEvaluatorTest.scala:133,137,144-148 also decodes 11544748 and 11544518 and asserts their txCount. No assertion is lost.

findings.claim: Interop's CCL -> Plutus ScriptContext path (getTxInfoV1/V2/V3, getScriptPurposeV1/V2/V3, getTxCertV3, getScriptContextV2/V3, getInterval, getDCert) has no unit test: it holds most of the 1043 uncovered statements of Interop.scala in the baseline (getTxCertV3 114, getScriptPurposeV3 68, getGovernanceActionV3 59, getTxInfoV3 44, ...). Only the integration module reaches parts of it. An oracle exists in scalus-core: LedgerToPlutusTranslation.getScriptContextV1/V2/V3 builds the same context from the Scalus Transaction.

Report each divergence as a finding before pinning.

findings.claim: '100_4x4_experiment_copy' has the same body as '100_4x4' (its comment says so) without the budget assertion; it was a debugging aid to compare call sites at two source positions. It asserts a subset of 100_4x4 and costs 0.72 s.
findings.coverageRisk: none: 100_4x4 compiles the same code and asserts success plus budget
findings.verification:
KnightsTest.scala:112-123 has the same compile body as 100_4x4 (lines 74-80): `runKnights(100, 4)` then `require(result === List.empty)`. It uses the same `toUplc(optimizeUplc = true)`, the same `evalWithOptionalProfile`, and the same class-level given Options. It asserts only `result.isSuccess`, which 100_4x4 also asserts at line 98, together with the budget and the reference comparison.

It was added in commit 9279dac8e as a debugging aid. Its own comment says it only compares call sites at two source positions; it asserts nothing about position independence. Deleting it loses no assertion.

findings.claim: Three tests compile runKnights(100, 4) with optimizeUplc = false. 217 asserts only success of .length; 247 asserts only success of (result === empty ? 1 : 0); 258 runs require(result === List.empty) and asserts success, which implies both others.
findings.action: Delete the tests at 217-222 and 247-256; keep 258-270 (rename it, the 'verbatim copy' comment is stale).
findings.coverageRisk: low: the .length path at depth 100 is not compiled any more; .length on the same list stays covered at smaller depths (C15-14)
findings.verification:
KnightsTestMinimal.scala has three tests, all with `optimizeUplc = false`:
- Line 217 compiles `runKnights(BigInt(100), BigInt(4)).length` and asserts only Success with evaluateDebug.
- Line 247 compiles `if result === expected then 1 else 0` and asserts only Success, accepting either branch.
- Line 258 compiles `require(runKnights(100,4) === List.empty)` and asserts `isSuccess` with evaluateProfile.

Success at line 258 means the same `===` comparison ran without a crash and returned true. That is stronger than line 247, which also accepts false. It also means the result is the empty list, so line 217's `.length` at depth 100 only takes the length of Nil.

Two small differences remain:
- The surviving test uses evaluateProfile, not evaluateDebug. The CEK semantics are the same.
- `.length` on the runKnights result is no longer compiled at depth 100. It stays covered at depths 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 (lines 176-211), and `===` with evaluateDebug stays covered at depth 1 (line 223).

No assertion is lost.

findings.claim: Six copy-pasted 'find the failing depth' tests (depth 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50) assert only that evaluation succeeds; 224-236 says 'either 0 or 1 is fine'. The values are known: a 4x4 board has no closed tour, so runKnights(d, 4) is empty for every d (KnightsTest.100_4x4 pins that for d = 100) and result === List.empty is 1. A lowering bug that returns a wrong list length still passes.
findings.action: Replace 175-215 with one loop: for d <- Seq(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50) do test(s"runKnights depth=$d size=4 is empty") { assertBigIntResult(compile { runKnights(BigInt(d), BigInt(4)).length }, 0) } (d must become a compile-time param or a Data arg; if compile{} cannot capture d, apply it as an argument). Make 224-236 assertBigIntResult(sir, 1).

findings.claim: KnightsTest checks budgets with a 5% tolerance (assertBudgetClose, 500 bps), so a budget regression of up to 5% in the UplcConstr lowering of 4x4, 6x6 or 8x8 (up to 7.6 G steps on 8x8) passes. KnightsDataTest and ClausifyTest pin exact budgets per compiler generation with ScalaCompilerVersion.baseline(pre38, since38). The comment ties the tolerance to CSE tie order, which is now deterministic (traversal order).
findings.action: Replace assertBudgetClose with exact pins via ScalaCompilerVersion.baseline for the three tests (measure on 3.3.8 and 3.9.0), drop ignoreBudgetAssertions and assertBudgetClose.
findings.coverageRisk: none: stricter; risk is only pin churn on compiler changes

findings.claim: Each benchmark selects its budget from summon[Options], but the suite's given Options is a constant with targetProtocolVersion = vanRossemPV, so only the first branch is live; the SirToUplcV3/SumOfProducts/Scott branches (with 'not tested' and 'actually we don't know' placeholders) are dead. Constant flags (printComparison, profilingEnabled, ignoreBudgetAssertions, isAlwaysPrintComparison, which is unused), commented budgets (ClausifyTest 1104, 1134) and commented lowering code (KnightsDataTest 58-59) add noise. All 11 tests repeat the same tail: assert success, assert budget, compareBudgetWithReferenceValue.
findings.action: Keep only the live pin in each test. Add one private helper per suite, checkBenchmark(name, result, expected: ExUnits, ref: ExUnits), that asserts success and budget and prints the comparison. Delete the constant flags (keep profiling as a local switch only if the owner wants it) and commented code.
findings.coverageRisk: none: the dead branches never run

findings.claim: ClausifyTest F4 spells its 32-clause expected result as a hand-nested Cons chain that scalafmt expands to one parenthesis per line: about 940 of the file's 1296 lines. compile{} accepts List(...) varargs (KnightsTest builds its expected tours with List(Tile(...), ...)).
findings.action: Rewrite F4's expected value as List[LRVars]((List(1), List(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7)), ...) inside // format: off, one clause per line. Re-measure and re-pin F4's budget (both baselines) if the UPLC of the literal changes.
findings.coverageRisk: low: the clause list is the same; the F4 budget pin and its ratio to the Plutus reference may shift slightly

findings.claim: Small style nits: InteropMapOrderingTest and ScalusScriptUtilsTest use a braceless class body (the style guide asks for {} on top-level definitions); BlueprintLayoutTest:45-49 is hand-wrapped and exceeds 100 columns at 49; BlueprintLayoutTest.tempDir uses deleteOnExit, which does not delete a non-empty directory, and StakeStateResolverTest.cache never deletes its temp directory, so each run leaks temp dirs.
findings.action: Use braces in the two classes; run scalafmt on the sbt plugin test; create temp dirs in a helper that deletes them recursively after the test (e.g. a withTempDir loan helper).
